description: Representing the KES Astronomy Team, our group entered the NASA Space Apps Challenge driven by a shared curiosity for the cosmos and a passion for collaborative problem-solving. Beyond working through our challenge track, we approached this weekend with a focus on community—meeting new people, exchanging perspectives with creative minds, and embracing the fun of rapid innovation under pressure.
summary: Our project, **Lunar Navigator**, aims to make the complexities of lunar exploration and mission planning understandable and engaging for everyone, regardless of age or scientific background. We developed an interactive platform that brings together the history, science, and engineering behind lunar missions in one accessible destination. Users can explore historical lunar missions, discover landing locations, and understand the different stages and challenges involved in reaching the Moon. By presenting complex aerospace concepts through interactive visualisations, detailed information, and engaging educational content, we bridge the gap between advanced space science and public understanding. Our goal is not only to educate the next generation of space enthusiasts but also to provide an accessible learning resource for aspiring engineers, students, educators, and future mission planners. We believe that understanding how difficult it is to reach the Moon is the first step towards inspiring those who will make future lunar exploration possible.
details:
Kestronomy is an interactive lunar mission planning and educational platform designed to break down the complexities of reaching and exploring the Moon. Rather than presenting space exploration as a collection of scientific facts, we allow users to experience a lunar mission through four specialist perspectives: Aerospace Engineer, Data Analyst, Astrophysicist and Astronaut.

The Aerospace Engineer section allows users to explore different rockets through interactive 3D models, understand rocket thrust and experiment with the rocket equation through a fuel-burn simulation. The Data Analyst perspective introduces the importance of Earth and environmental data in mission planning. The Astrophysicist perspective explores orbital mechanics, launch opportunities and the science behind reaching the Moon. Finally, the Astronaut section allows users to experience lunar surface operations and attempt their own lunar landing through interactive simulations and a student-developed 3D game.

We also developed an interactive lunar mission archive featuring 125 historical missions and attempts. Users can rotate the lunar globe, select landing locations, explore mission information and travel through the history of lunar exploration.

Our greatest benefit is making advanced aerospace concepts accessible to people who may have never studied physics or engineering. By combining scientific information with simulations, interactive models, historical data and game-based learning, we transform passive learning into active experimentation.

Our intended impact is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers and astronauts while helping students, educators and aspiring mission planners understand the multidisciplinary challenges of lunar exploration. We want Kestronomy to become a starting point for anyone curious about humanity's return to the Moon.

Creativity was central to our approach. Instead of developing another conventional educational website, we created an experience in which users become part of the mission. Each specialist perspective represents a different real-world discipline, demonstrating how aerospace engineers, data analysts, astrophysicists and astronauts must collaborate to achieve a successful lunar landing.

Throughout development, our team considered scientific accuracy, accessibility across different age groups, user engagement, ease of navigation, the limitations of simplified simulations and the importance of distinguishing educational models from real mission predictions. We also incorporated publicly available NASA scientific resources and historical mission information to ground the experience in real space exploration.

The platform was developed as a WordPress-based website, incorporating interactive web experiences, simulations, 3D visualisations and a student-developed 3D game. We also used Higgsfield-generated 3D rocket illustrations to help users visualise different launch vehicles. Our priority was to combine technology, scientific understanding and storytelling into one accessible learning environment.
